messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

When Malik was eight years old, the domestic violence in the adjacent apartment shattered his understanding of safety. He remembers the precise moment the shouting began, the splintering of a chair back, and the sharp glint of a kitchen knife caught in the hallway light. What frightened him most was the sudden, suffocating silence that followed—the kind of quiet that always preceded a blow he knew was coming. His young body had locked against the cold plaster, pressing into the corner just to keep still. That night etched itself into him as a series of frozen snapshots; even now, he recalls the scene not as a continuous narrative, but as a few stark pictures in his mind, each one carrying the full weight of the original terror. Now eighteen and working as a patrol officer, Malik navigates a world that constantly reactivates those early imprints. He walks the same familiar beat daily because he had come to believe he could not rely on himself to assess an unfamiliar area for danger. During a foot patrol near the precinct’s eastern sector, he found himself tracing the edges of every parked vehicle for hidden objects, his gaze locked on potential weapons or dangerous objects whenever his eyes drifted from the sidewalk. Whenever he feels a baseline of discomfort or notices someone acting suspiciously on the street, his mind instantly pulls him back to the neighbor’s kitchen. Those involuntary intrusions are accompanied by a physical jolt; his posture mimics the exact position he held as a child, and the overwhelming grief that surfaces leaves him breathless. His conviction that he is going crazy, combined with his fear that he is utterly helpless to stop bad things from happening, makes him hypersensitive to ordinary cues. Because he doubts his own stability, he interprets every glance and every shift in tone as a prelude to violence. This self-doubt fuels a relentless cycle. The intrusive memories themselves seem to dictate his reactions, causing him to flinch at sudden movements or feel entirely unprepared when a colleague pats his shoulder unexpectedly. Once those memories surface, they transform his present environment, making him fixate on potential weapons or dangerous objects wherever he walks. His constant vigilance against perceived danger, in turn, keeps the old memories fresh, ensuring they never fade into the background. Living in a state of constant alarm eroded his confidence further, reinforcing the thought that he was helpless to protect anyone, including himself. Because he feels so powerless, he avoids stepping into unknown precincts or detours, since navigating uncharted territory strips away his ability to track danger. The more he isolates himself in familiar zones, the more his mind waits for disaster, which in turn makes him more sensitive to any hint of unpredictability. His score of 77 on the standardized inventory mirrored the intensity of this daily hyperarousal. By the time he sought help, his routine had collapsed; he could no longer complete full shifts without leaving early, and his emotional withdrawal from his partner had drawn a formal command warning. He came to the clinic hoping to quiet the grief, to steady his hands, and to find a way to live without bracing for the next blow.
